analysis.one_liner: Changes how the minimum wage for farm guest workers is calculated, generally lowering it.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on December 18, 2025 with one cosponsor and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The federal government sets a minimum wage, called the adverse effect wage rate, that farms must pay H-2A guest workers — and it also sets the floor for U.S. workers doing the same farm jobs. Today that rate is calculated from a Department of Agriculture survey of farm wages. This bill would instead base it on the Bureau of Labor Statistics' broader statewide wage survey covering all occupations, which generally produces a lower number. It would also let immigration authorities start processing guest worker petitions before the Labor Department finishes its review. Despite its title, the bill's main effect would be to lower the guaranteed wage floor for farmworkers and speed up the guest worker pipeline for employers.
analysis.who_benefits: Agricultural employers — especially growers of labor-intensive crops like fruits, vegetables, and nursery stock that rely on H-2A guest workers — would gain twice: a lower guaranteed wage floor cuts their largest cost, and letting petition processing start before Labor certification shortens the wait to bring workers in. Growers' associations have long argued the current rate, calculated from a survey of farm wages, has climbed too fast and squeezes small farms.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Farms that hire H-2A guest workers

how_it_helps.text: It changes the wage formula for H-2A guest workers from the current method (which relies on a USDA farm wage survey) to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' statewide all-occupation wage estimates, a broader measure that typically produces lower required wage rates.

It lets the Department of Homeland Security begin processing H-2A worker petitions at the same time the Department of Labor reviews the labor certification, instead of in sequence, shortening the wait for employers to bring guest workers in.

analysis.who_pays: H-2A guest workers and the U.S. farmworkers who work the same jobs. The adverse effect wage rate is the legal minimum under their pay; recalculating it from a broader statewide survey would generally lower that floor, which flows straight into the take-home pay of some of the country's lowest-wage workers.

drawbacks.text: Switching the adverse effect wage rate to the broader Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics survey would generally produce a lower wage floor than the current farm-specific calculation, cutting pay for the guest workers it covers and for U.S. workers employed alongside them in the same jobs.

Letting the Department of Homeland Security begin processing H-2A petitions before the Department of Labor certifies that U.S. workers will not be adversely affected short-circuits the existing labor-certification check.

Supporters' strongest case: the current adverse effect wage rate is based on a survey of farm employers' own wage reports that has risen sharply, and it imposes real costs on small farms that then get passed into food prices — an honest supporter would acknowledge the trade-off is between grower costs and the pay of the lowest-wage workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real relief to growers facing high and rising AEWR rates and slow H-2A processing, and supporters argue the current wage formula relies on a survey that overstates market wages and squeezes small farms. But the costs fall entirely on the lowest-paid workers in the country: a lower wage floor for guest workers tends to pull down pay for U.S. farm crews in the same jobs, and the "Fair Wages for Farmworkers" title points the opposite way from the bill's likely effect. On balance, the benefits are concentrated and the costs are diffuse but fall on people with little bargaining power.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-December 2025 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a vote, or any movement since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 18, 2025 by Rep. Monica De La Cruz, with Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar joining as the bill's one cosponsor.
Its only action since introduction is a referral to the House Judiciary Committee on the same day; no hearing, markup, or floor vote has occurred.

The bill directs the Labor Secretary to set the H-2A adverse effect wage rate using statewide all-occupation wage survey data, and lets Homeland Security begin processing H-2A petitions before the Labor Department finishes its certification.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has moved it, so the current higher wage floor for farmworkers remains in place — farmworkers are, for now, no worse off. Agricultural employers pushing to lower the wage rate have not yet gotten the change they sought.

for.name: Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's original and only cosponsor

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 18, 2025; no hearing or markup scheduled since

sides.party_line_note: Only two Republicans have put their names on it so far, and no member of either party has voted or spoken against it; the partisan shape of the fight has not formed yet.

industries.industry: Agricultural employers (farms hiring H-2A guest workers)
industries.note: A lower adverse effect wage rate directly cuts the wage these employers must guarantee, and concurrent petition processing shortens the pipeline for bringing in labor. The savings come out of pay for farmworkers, including U.S. workers in the same jobs.

industries.industry: Farmworkers (H-2A guest workers and U.S. field crews)
industries.note: The adverse effect wage rate is the legal floor under their pay; recalculating it from a broader survey would generally lower that floor, and U.S. crews protected by the same standard would feel it too. This group is the bill's direct cost-bearer despite the bill's title.
Lower farm labor costs can eventually trim input costs, but the effect is indirect and small at the shelf price level, and it arrives by way of lower farmworker pay.

analysis.trajectory: With a single cosponsor and no committee action since its December 2025 referral, the bill is very likely to sit in the House Judiciary Committee until the Congress ends. Changes to the H-2A wage formula that farm-employer groups favor have historically had better odds attached to a broader agriculture or spending bill than as standalone legislation, so if anything moves this Congress it would probably not be this bill on its own.
